title: Topological task sorting for orchestration
description: Topological sorting orders archive tasks so every task runs only after all of its dependencies have completed. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes tasks with zero remaining in-degree, appending them to the execution order; any tasks left over at the end reveal a dependency cycle. The orchestrator uses this order as the master schedule for a whole archive pipeline. Use it whenever a multi-stage archive job (harvest, index, verify, publish) must run in a provably safe order.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: DAG dependency validation and cycle detection
title: DAG dependency validation and cycle detection
description: Dependency validation checks an archive task graph for cycles before any work is scheduled, because a cycle makes orchestration impossible. A depth-first search marks each node white, gray, or black; encountering a gray node during the search proves a cycle exists, and the search path names the exact loop. The orchestrator rejects or quarantines cyclic graphs with the offending chain reported. Use it as a pre-flight gate on every generated or imported pipeline definition.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Parallel frontier scheduling across worker pools
title: Parallel frontier scheduling across worker pools
description: Frontier scheduling keeps a ready-set of tasks whose dependencies are all done and dispatches them to workers the moment a slot frees up. The orchestrator maintains the frontier as a queue; each completion event re-examines blocked tasks and promotes newly-ready ones, so independent branches run in parallel while dependent chains stay ordered. This achieves the maximum parallelism the DAG allows without any worker idling unnecessarily. Use it to squeeze the shortest possible wall-clock time out of a dependency graph.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Work-stealing queues for dynamic load balance
title: Work-stealing queues for dynamic load balance
description: Work-stealing gives every worker its own double-ended queue of tasks, and idle workers steal work from the back of busy workers' queues. Each worker pushes and pops from the front of its own deque with no locking contention on the hot path; a thief takes from the tail, which holds the oldest, coarsest tasks and minimizes further stealing. This dynamically balances highly irregular archive workloads without a central scheduler bottleneck. Use it when task costs vary wildly, such as indexing archives of mixed document sizes.
demo:
import collections, random
random.seed(7)
queues = [collections.deque(range(i * 5, i * 5 + 5)) for i in range(3)]
stolen = 0
for _ in range(40):
    w = random.randrange(3)
    if queues[w]:
        queues[w].popleft()
    else:
        victim = max(range(3), key=lambda v: len(queues[v]))
        if queues[victim]:
            queues[victim].pop(); stolen += 1
print("Tasks stolen for balance:", stolen)
print("Remaining per worker:", [len(q) for q in queues])

t: Priority-queue scheduling with aging against starvation
title: Priority-queue scheduling with aging against starvation
description: Priority scheduling always runs the most important ready task next, while aging gradually boosts long-waiting tasks so nothing starves. Ready tasks sit in a binary heap keyed by effective priority; on every tick each waiting task's key improves slightly, guaranteeing that even the lowest-priority archive job eventually outranks newcomers. The orchestrator uses it to honor service-level promises while keeping background work moving. Use it to mix urgent user queries with long background archive builds on one cluster.
demo:
import heapq, itertools
counter = itertools.count()
heap = []
def push(name, prio): heapq.heappush(heap, (-prio, next(counter), name, 0))
push("user-query", 10); push("nightly-index", 2); push("verify", 5)
ran = []
for tick in range(3):
    heap = [(-p - 1, c, n, w + 1) for (p, c, n, w) in heap]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    p, c, name, w = heapq.heappop(heap); ran.append((name, w))
print("Run order (name, ticks waited):", ran)

t: Backpressure flow control between pipeline stages
title: Backpressure flow control between pipeline stages
description: Backpressure lets a slow downstream stage signal upstream stages to pause instead of letting unbounded queues eat all memory. Each stage owns a bounded queue; when the queue is full the producer blocks or sheds load rather than enqueueing, which propagates the slowdown cleanly up the pipeline. The orchestrator monitors queue depths and can also shed the lowest-value work first when pressure persists. Use it in every streaming archive pipeline so one slow sink cannot crash the whole job.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Exponential backoff with jitter for retried operations
title: Exponential backoff with jitter for retried operations
description: Exponential backoff retries a failed archive operation after waits that double each attempt, with random jitter to stop synchronized retries from stampeding. The wait before attempt n is base * 2^n plus a random fraction; the orchestrator caps the wait and the attempt count, then routes the task to a dead-letter queue with its failure history. Jitter decorrelates thousands of clients so a recovering service is not hit by a thundering herd. Use it for every network call to an archive source or storage backend.
demo:
import random
random.seed(3)
base, cap, attempts = 0.5, 8.0, 5
waits = [min(cap, base * (2 ** n)) + random.uniform(0, 0.5) for n in range(attempts)]
print("Retry waits (s):", [round(w, 2) for w in waits])
assert all(waits[i] <= waits[i+1] + 0.5 for i in range(len(waits)-1))
print("Growing with jitter: OK")
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Checkpoint and resume for long-running archive jobs
title: Checkpoint and resume for long-running archive jobs
description: Checkpointing periodically persists the full progress state of a job so a crash resumes from the last checkpoint instead of restarting from zero. The orchestrator writes checkpoints atomically (write-temp-then-rename) at task boundaries and records them in a journal; on restart it replays the journal, skips completed tasks, and re-queues only the interrupted one. Checkpoint frequency trades a little I/O overhead against the cost of rework. Use it for any archive build that runs longer than a few minutes.
demo:
import json, os
CKPT = "/tmp/t1_ckpt.json"
state = {"done": ["fetch", "parse"], "next": 2}  # crashed after 2 tasks
tasks = ["fetch", "parse", "index", "verify", "publish"]
for i, t in enumerate(tasks[2:], start=2):
    state["done"].append(t); state["next"] = i + 1
    open(CKPT + ".tmp", "w").write(json.dumps(state)); os.replace(CKPT + ".tmp", CKPT)
    break  # crash right after checkpointing 'index'
recovered = json.load(open(CKPT))
print("Recovered:", recovered)
remaining = [t for t in tasks if t not in recovered["done"]]
print("Resume with:", remaining)
assert remaining == ["verify", "publish"]; os.remove(CKPT)

t: Circuit breaker for failing downstream services
title: Circuit breaker for failing downstream services
description: A circuit breaker stops calling a service that is failing, fails fast instead, and periodically lets one probe through to detect recovery. The breaker counts consecutive failures; past a threshold it opens and rejects calls immediately for a cooldown, then enters half-open state where a single trial call decides whether to close again. This prevents cascade failures and gives the downstream service room to recover. Use it around every external archive dependency the orchestrator calls.
demo:
class Breaker:
    def __init__(s, limit=3, cool=2): s.limit, s.cool, s.fails, s.open, s.cd = limit, cool, 0, False, 0
    def call(s, fn):
        if s.open:
            s.cd -= 1
            if s.cd <= 0: s.open = False; s.fails = 0
            else: return "fast-fail"
        try: r = fn(); s.fails = 0; return r
        except Exception: s.fails += 1
        if s.fails >= s.limit: s.open, s.cd = True, s.cool
        return "error"
b = Breaker()
down = lambda: (_ for _ in ()).throw(IOError("down"))
print([b.call(down) for _ in range(6)])
print("Breaker open, failing fast:", b.open)

title: Resource-aware scheduling with bin-packing fit
description: Resource-aware scheduling places each task on the worker node whose remaining CPU and memory best fit the task's declared requirements. The orchestrator treats nodes as bins with two dimensions (CPU, RAM) and uses a best-fit heuristic: the task goes to the node where it leaves the least leftover slack, keeping fragmentation low. Tasks that fit nowhere wait in a pending queue instead of being force-placed. Use it to run mixed archive workloads at high utilization without overcommitting nodes.
demo:
nodes = [{"cpu": 8, "mem": 32}, {"cpu": 4, "mem": 16}]
tasks = [("index-big", 6, 24), ("verify", 2, 4), ("parse", 3, 8)]
placed = {}
for name, cpu, mem in tasks:
    fits = [(i, (n["cpu"]-cpu) + (n["mem"]-mem)) for i, n in enumerate(nodes)
            if n["cpu"] >= cpu and n["mem"] >= mem]
    if fits:
        i = min(fits, key=lambda f: f[1])[0]
        nodes[i]["cpu"] -= cpu; nodes[i]["mem"] -= mem; placed[name] = i
print("Placement:", placed)
print("Leftover:", nodes)
assert placed["index-big"] == 0
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Token-bucket quota enforcement per archive tenant
title: Token-bucket quota enforcement per archive tenant
description: A token bucket meters each tenant's archive operations: tokens refill at a fixed rate and every operation spends tokens, so bursts are allowed but sustained rate is capped. The orchestrator keeps one bucket per tenant with capacity C and refill rate R; an operation of cost k proceeds only if the bucket holds k tokens, otherwise it waits or is rejected. This gives smooth, fair sharing of harvest and indexing capacity across tenants. Use it to protect shared archive infrastructure from any single heavy user.
demo:
import time
class Bucket:
    def __init__(s, cap, rate): s.cap, s.rate, s.tok, s.t = cap, rate, cap, time.monotonic()
    def take(s, k=1):
        now = time.monotonic(); s.tok = min(s.cap, s.tok + (now - s.t) * s.rate); s.t = now
        if s.tok >= k: s.tok -= k; return True
        return False
b = Bucket(5, 5)
ok = sum(b.take() for _ in range(8))
print("Immediate grants out of 8:", ok, "(bucket caps the burst at 5)")
assert ok == 5

title: Graceful degradation with cached fallbacks
description: Graceful degradation keeps the archive answering queries at reduced fidelity when backends are overloaded, instead of failing outright. The orchestrator defines service tiers: full live results, then stale-cache results, then static summaries; when latency or error budgets trip, it steps down a tier and labels the response with its freshness. Users get answers with honest staleness rather than timeouts. Use it so archive search stays up during index rebuilds or traffic spikes.
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

title: Saga pattern for multi-archive transactions
description: The saga pattern coordinates a transaction across several archive stores as a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action that undoes it on failure. The orchestrator runs steps in order and records each completion; if a later step fails it executes the compensations in reverse, restoring every store to its prior state. This gives atomic-like behavior across systems that cannot share one database transaction. Use it when one logical archive update must touch the index, the blob store, and the manifest together.
demo:
log = []
def step(name, comp): log.append(name); return comp
comps = []
try:
    comps.append(step("write-blob", lambda: log.append("undo-blob")))
    comps.append(step("update-index", lambda: log.append("undo-index")))
    raise IOError("manifest store down")
    comps.append(step("update-manifest", lambda: log.append("undo-manifest")))
except IOError as e:
    for c in reversed(comps): c()
print("Saga log:", log)
assert log == ["write-blob", "update-index", "undo-index", "undo-blob"]
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Leader election for single-writer archive coordination
title: Leader election for single-writer archive coordination
description: Leader election picks exactly one orchestrator instance as the writer for a shared archive so concurrent writers never corrupt it. In the bully variant each instance knows the others' IDs; the highest live ID wins, and instances probe higher IDs with timeouts before declaring themselves leader. Heartbeats from the leader suppress new elections until it actually fails. Use it whenever archive writers run redundantly for high availability.
demo:
import random
random.seed(11)
ids = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
alive = {i: random.random() > 0.3 for i in ids}
alive[max(ids)] = True
leader = max(i for i in ids if alive[i])
print("Alive:", alive, "-> leader:", leader)
assert leader == max(i for i in ids if alive[i])
provenance: public-harvest: established computer-science methods documented in standard literature and practice

t: Distributed tracing spans across orchestrated stages
title: Distributed tracing spans across orchestrated stages
description: Distributed tracing follows one archive job across every stage by passing a trace context that each stage extends with its own timed span. The orchestrator injects a trace ID and parent-span ID into each task's metadata; stages record start/end timestamps and status, and the collector stitches spans into a waterfall. Slow or failing stages become visible instead of hiding inside a total duration. Use it to find which stage of a long archive pipeline is actually slow.
demo:
import time
trace, spans = "trace-1", []
def span(name, parent, dur):
    spans.append({"trace": trace, "name": name, "parent": parent, "dur_ms": dur})
span("harvest", None, 120); span("index", "harvest", 340); span("verify", "index", 45)
slowest = max(spans, key=lambda s: s["dur_ms"])
print("Slowest stage:", slowest["name"], slowest["dur_ms"], "ms")
for s in spans: print(f'  {s["name"]} <- {s["parent"]}: {s["dur_ms"]}ms')
assert slowest["name"] == "index"
